title: Derive the tier from tracker facts instead of choosing it per dispatch
description:
Stop the orchestrator CHOOSING a tier and make it DERIVE one. Today the tier is
a per-dispatch judgement call by a model (`tk herd spawn <id> --role implement
--tier strong`), which is how a run ends up on an advanced tier that nothing
justified. Same tick, same graph position, different day, different model.

The design line this tick must hold: the tracker describes the WORK, ticfac owns
the MAPPING from a description to a dispatch. No orchestration config moves into
ticks.

INPUTS — tracker facts that already exist and are legitimately the tracker's.
ticfac's tk client already decodes them (internal/tk/tk.go:821,824): priority,
type, the process role (review/closeout), labels, and the tick's position in the
graph (is it a wave-1 tick, does it block others, how many). Nothing new is
added to a tick, and no field is invented in ticks.

POLICY — a declared table in ticfac, evaluated, not judged. It belongs with the
execution half of the routing config, which is why this tick is blocked behind
the config split (wgi): the roles and tiers tables must be ticfac's before a
policy can sit beside them. Resolution stays internal/profile's — routing must
never become a second way to authorise a command line.

ESCALATION — the part that actually fixes the complaint. A first attempt starts
at the DEFAULT tier. Only a failed attempt escalates, by declared rule, bounded
(e.g. one step per attempt, never past a named ceiling). Nothing can start high
on a hunch; expense is earned by evidence. Decide and log the exact ladder and
what "failed" means for it — a refusal, a gate failure, an escalation to a
human are not the same thing.

OVERRIDE — via a LABEL, not a new tracker field. A label is an opaque string to
ticks: it stores it and has no idea what it means. ticfac assigns the meaning
and REFUSES an unrecognised tier label loudly, naming the tick and the label,
the same discipline the rest of this epic uses. The honest cost, to be written
down: a label is a weakly typed field, ticks cannot validate it, and a typo only
surfaces at dispatch — which is why the refusal must be loud rather than a
silent fall-back to the default.

TWO PREREQUISITES, both in scope here:
1. Record the TIER in provenance. It is not recorded today — Provenance carries
   Role, Model and ProfileDigest (internal/runstate/records.go:36-38) and no
   tier. So there is currently no way to audit which tier a dispatch used, only
   which model came out of it. That is part of why an over-tiered run is hard to
   catch after the fact.
2. Make the derivation a PURE FUNCTION of (tick facts, attempt number, policy).
   No clock, no randomness, no model call. That is what makes the property
   testable rather than aspirational.

Interaction to respect: the budget clamp already adjusts what a run may spend.
Say explicitly which wins when the policy asks for a tier the budget refuses,
and make that refusal legible rather than a silent downgrade.

## Concurrency is a PROVIDER property, not a host one

Found the hard way on wave 2, 2026-09-10. Four concurrent GLM-5.3 workers on
cloudflare Workers AI: one (jv7) hit HTTP 429 with no body, pi retried three
times with NO BACKOFF, gave up, and the tick sat dead until a person noticed.
The other three never saw a 429 at all.

Cloudflare publishes a per-account requests-per-minute cap for Workers AI
(developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/platform/limits). An agent in a tool loop
makes many requests per minute, so four workers can exceed an account cap in
bursts while any one of them alone stays under it.

`[orchestration].max_parallel` is today a single number describing what the HOST
can carry. That is the wrong axis once a tier names a provider: four claude
workers and four cloudflare workers are not the same load on the same limit. The
policy this tick declares should carry a concurrency bound PER PROVIDER (or per
tier), so routing a wave to cloudflare narrows the width automatically instead of
relying on an operator to remember.

And the failure mode matters as much as the number: a 429 is a transient burst
limit, and retrying three times immediately converts it into a dead worker. Say
explicitly what the run does on a rate limit — back off and retry is a pause; not
doing so is a stall. This is the same fail-open-to-a-stall shape the rest of the
epic is chasing.
notes: 2026-09-11 17:37 - runner-state: dispatched on pi/cloudflare GLM-5.3 effort=high from base dd845cb, with pi retry now configured for the cloudflare 429 (8 attempts, 90s ceiling)
acceptance_criteria: Tier selection is a pure function of tick facts, attempt number and a declared ticfac-side policy: the same tick at the same attempt always derives the same tier, asserted by a test that calls it twice and by a table test over priority, type, role and graph position. No new field is added to a tick and no orchestration config lives in ticks. A first attempt uses the default tier; escalation happens only on a failed attempt, is bounded by a named ceiling, and the ladder plus the definition of 'failed' is a logged decision. An override label is honoured, and an unrecognised tier label is refused loudly naming the tick and the label rather than falling back to the default. Every dispatch records its tier in provenance alongside role, model and profile digest. Where the budget clamp refuses the derived tier, the outcome is stated rather than silently downgraded. go test -short -timeout 45m ./... green (make test-short). The declared policy carries a concurrency bound per provider or per tier rather than one host-wide number, so a wave routed to a rate-limited provider narrows automatically; and what the run does on a provider rate limit is stated — a 429 backs off and retries rather than being retried immediately and abandoned.
closed_reason: DONE_WITH_CONCERNS, concern verified and accepted as a residual. Tier derivation is a pure function of tracker facts, attempt number and a declared policy; an unrecognised tier label is refused loudly; a first attempt takes the default and only a failed attempt escalates. The concern is accurate, checked in code rather than taken on trust: the derived tier IS carried durably on the dispatch marker (dispatch.go:72,83,109) but is NOT a field of the pinned Provenance object (internal/runstate/records.go has no tier), so 'recorded in provenance' is met through the marker and the tier-resolved profile digest rather than literally. Putting it inside Provenance needs an upstream ticks contract-bundle bump, which is out of a worker's reach by design — the same boundary 8ug hit. Routed to tick 9t0, which owns the bundle bump. Full uncached gate green at 179s.
